doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

chapter: Swing, hot jazz and the bebop split
title: Who fanned the moldy fig feud; his love of the Chicago school
summary: Younger musicians and critics promoted the feud; he favored Sullivan, Teschemacher, Freeman, Tough, Wettling and Fats Waller.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Many musicians felt, younger ones, yeah I think they had a lot to do with it. They fanned the flames. They saw good copy. Divide and— bebop versus— they even use to have those concerts at Birdland. The moldy figs. Here’s Max Kaminsky and Edmond Hall and who else and whatever. And over here are Diz and Bird or whatever it is. You know, and this is going to get people to come in. It’s sort of like that trumped up, like the boxing thing, you know when they all, “I can knock ‘em flat” and all that stuff. You know, hokey kind of stuff. But no, I liked, when I say “hot music” hot music to me was, I was especially fond for some reason that I can’t define, I would just latch on to certain things. I especially was fond of the Chicago guys. Joe Sullivan, Teschemacker, Bud, those guys, that whole school. Dave Tough, Wettling, all those guys. I was very fond of them. And they were like the fobbs. Later on it occurred to me they were the first really middle class, high school kids type guys who really embraced jazz as a group. They and Bix and a few others. Otherwise jazz sort of came, if you pardon the expression, it was sort of considered as coming from the wrong side of the tracks you know. But that’s not why. And I always loved of course, I always loved Fats, who I considered a hot player. These were hot players, you know. Herman Autrey, who I rarely got a chance to play with, and guys like that. But I always felt that my allegiance, just my physical type, the way, something—I like hot music. I’m not necessarily, that doesn’t mean you hate the other stuff, but it’s just not what really grabs you. It’s not the path you would choose to follow.
